Achilles. The mightiest warrior of the Trojan War and nearly invulnerable, unmatched in combat prowess. He was the son of Thetis, a sea-nymph, and Peleus, a mortal king, representing the apex of martial excellence and also the tragedy of a life cut short by glory.

His mother made him nearly invulnerable as an infant by dipping him in the river Styx. But she held him by his heel, leaving that one spot exposed and vulnerable. From childhood, he was trained by the wise centaur Chiron in the arts of war, medicine, and wisdom. Yet Achilles understood his fate. He could choose between two paths—a long life lived quietly, forgotten in obscurity, or a short life that would burn with glory and be remembered forever. He chose glory.

At Troy, he became the greatest warrior the Greeks possessed. He slew countless Trojan soldiers and their champions throughout the ten-year siege, his name synonymous with martial excellence. But his pride and his wrath nearly cost the Greeks the entire war. When Agamemnon, the commander of the Greek forces, seized a captive woman named Briseis, Achilles saw it as a personal insult and withdrew from battle in protest. With their mightiest warrior absent, the Greeks suffered devastating losses, nearly tipping the war toward defeat.

Achilles remained in his camp until his closest companion, Patroclus, was killed by the Trojan champion Hector while wearing Achilles' own armor. The news drove him into a fury. He returned to the battlefield to avenge his beloved companion, and the turning point had come. He killed Hector in single combat and then, consumed by rage and grief, he dragged Hector's corpse around the walls of Troy three times, dishonoring his fallen enemy in a way that shocked even the other Greeks.

Yet Achilles himself would not see Troy's final fall. Paris, the Trojan prince, shot a poisoned arrow that found the one vulnerable part of his body—his heel. Achilles died, his short but glorious life complete, just as fate had promised. His death marked the beginning of Troy's collapse, though he did not live to witness the city's conquest.

His legacy transformed into something larger than any single battle. The term "Achilles' heel" became a metaphor for a hidden weakness in anything seemingly invulnerable, a phrase that still shapes how we think about vulnerability and fatal flaws. He stands at the foundation of Western heroic tradition, embodying the ancient ideal that a short life lived with honor surpasses a long one lived in obscurity.
